prose_changes.old: The Observance began small. In 1368 Paoluccio Trinci and a handful of friars kept the Rule strictly at Brugliano. Then it spread across the Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Benedictines alike. Its public face was preaching to great crowds. In 1427 Bernardino of Siena gave forty-five sermons, and a listener in the crowd took them down as he spoke, asides and all. It is about as close as anyone gets to hearing a medieval sermon, not just reading one. What it left is mixed. It left the low-interest pawn-banks called monti di pietà, which still trade today. But John of Capistrano's preaching also drove the persecution of Jewish communities. The most notorious case was at Breslau in 1453.

I, n. 1072) makes Capistrano enforcer of the decrees restricting Jews and Muslims in Italy, and Lea's index (vol. III) records Jews 'burned by Capistrano in Breslau'. 'Preaching' is dropped because neither source shows the preaching as the cause; the burning and the 1447 commission are added because the sources show them. Nothing is softened.

prose_changes.old: The Observance began as an argument inside the religious orders. Its friars said the Rule should be kept as it was written. It should not be kept as years of exceptions had relaxed it. It started small, with Paoluccio Trinci's handful of friars at Brugliano in 1368. Then it spread across the Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Benedictines alike. In the end, reformed houses formed rival provinces beside the unreformed ones. Its public face was preaching. Bernardino of Siena drew whole towns into the square to hear him for weeks on end. In 1427 he preached forty-five sermons at Siena. A listener in the crowd took them down as he spoke, with his asides and the crowd's reactions. It is about as close as anyone gets to hearing a medieval sermon, not just reading one. John of Capistrano did the same across central Europe. The movement's dark side belongs in the same story. Capistrano's preaching also drove the persecution of Jewish communities. The most notorious case was at Breslau in 1453.

prose_changes.old: The Rule became the standard for monks in the West. Carolingian reformers made it the norm across the Frankish empire. It stands behind the Cluniacs, the Cistercians and the Benedictine congregations that keep it today. Its language of stability, obedience and moderation reached far beyond the cloister. So did the way it built the day around fixed hours of prayer, and both passed into the West's habits of work and time. Monte Cassino itself was destroyed again and again — by Lombards, by Saracens, by earthquake, and by Allied bombing in 1944 — and rebuilt every time. Monks live there now.
prose_changes.new: The Rule became the standard for monks in the West. Carolingian reformers made it the norm across the Frankish empire. It stands behind the Cluniacs, the Cistercians and the Benedictine congregations that keep it today. Its language of stability, obedience and moderation reached far beyond the cloister. So did the way it built the day around fixed hours of prayer, and both passed into the West's habits of work and time. Monte Cassino itself was destroyed again and again, and rebuilt every time. Paul the Deacon tells how the Lombards sacked it. Later records add the Saracens, an earthquake, and Allied bombing in 1944. Monks live there now.
prose_changes.reason: Ruling 6 guard (violence charged to the Saracens and the Allies). The Lombard sack is sourced (Paul the Deacon IV.17); the Saracen attack, the earthquake and the bombing of 1944 have no source in the Library, so they are stated as what later records report. The rebuilding and today's monks stand as plain facts.

prose_changes.old: The Viking wars nearly destroyed English Christianity, and when Alfred of Wessex set out to rebuild it, he complained he could barely find a priest south of the Thames able to translate a Latin letter, so he launched a program translating essential books into English instead. A century later the bishops Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald refounded the monasteries on the Benedictine rule, and Ælfric wrote well over a hundred English sermons so ordinary congregations could hear careful teaching in their own tongue, while Archbishop Wulfstan, preaching in 1014 as Danish invasions closed in, told the English their own sins had brought the disaster on them.
prose_changes.new: In the Viking wars, by Alfred of Wessex's own account, England's churches were ravaged and burned. When he set out to rebuild, he complained he could barely find a priest south of the Thames able to translate a Latin letter. So he set out to put the books the clergy most needed into English. A century later the bishops Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald refounded the monasteries on the Rule of Benedict. Ælfric wrote English sermons, well over a hundred by his editors' count, so that ordinary people could hear sound teaching in their own tongue. Archbishop Wulfstan preached in 1014, as Danish invasions closed in. He told the English that their own sins had brought the disaster on them.
prose_changes.reason: Ruling 6 guard (violence; a count). The ravaging of the churches is put in Alfred's own words, from his preface to the Pastoral Care (wanted). Aelfric's 'well over a hundred' is a count with no source in the Library, so it is given as his editors' count. Long sentences split to meet the reading target; no other fact changed.

prose_changes.old: The Viking wars nearly killed English Christianity. Monasteries were destroyed, whole dioceses lapsed, and when Alfred of Wessex set out to rebuild he complained that he could hardly find a priest south of the Thames able to translate a Latin letter. His answer was a translation program — Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care and other essential books put into English so that clergy could read them at all. And the Chronicle begun in his reign is the first sustained history written in English. A century later a second rebuilding, led by the bishops Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald, refounded the monasteries on the Benedictine rule and produced an agreed customary for the whole country. The vernacular stayed central throughout: Ælfric wrote well over a hundred sermons in English so that ordinary congregations could hear careful teaching in their own tongue, and Archbishop Wulfstan, preaching in 1014 as the Danish invasions closed in, told the English that their own sins had brought the calamity on them. The Norman Conquest of 1066 ended the church's independent development.

prose_changes.old: Christianity came to Scandinavia through kings as much as missionaries — Harald Bluetooth raised a stone at Jelling claiming he had made the Danes Christian, and the Norwegian king Olaf Haraldsson was killed pressing the faith and venerated as a saint almost at once. Iceland took a different road: in the year 1000 the pagan law-speaker Þorgeir, after a night's deliberation, ruled at the island's own assembly that all Icelanders would be baptized, a whole community changing religion by public decision rather than by force.
prose_changes.new: Christianity came to Scandinavia through kings as much as missionaries. Harald Bluetooth raised a stone at Jelling claiming he had made the Danes Christian. The Norwegian king Olaf Haraldsson was killed in battle. He was honored as a saint almost at once, and later writers made him a martyr for the faith. Iceland took a different road. In the year 1000 the pagan law-speaker Þorgeir thought it over for a night. Then he ruled at the island's own assembly that all Icelanders would be baptized. A whole people changed its faith by public decision rather than by force.
prose_changes.reason: Ruling 6 guard (disputed). That Olaf Haraldsson was killed 'pressing the faith' is disputed: the battle of 1030 is now usually read as a revolt of his own magnates. The death in battle stands; the martyr reading is given as later writers' account. Sentences split to meet the reading target.

prose_changes.old: Christianity came north in fits and starts over nearly three centuries. A Frankish monk named Anskar preached in Denmark and at Birka in Sweden in the 820s and 830s, with modest and short-lived results. Then came the kings — Harald Bluetooth, who set up a great carved stone at Jelling claiming that he had 'made the Danes Christian', and the two Olafs in Norway, whose methods included force and one of whom was killed in battle and venerated as a saint almost at once. Iceland took a different road: in the year 1000 the question was put to the Althing, the island's assembly, and the pagan law-speaker Þorgeir, after a night's deliberation, ruled that all Icelanders should be baptized, with some old practices tolerated privately for a time — a whole community changing religion by public decision rather than by conquest. The window closes in 1104, when the northern church received its own archbishopric at Lund and stopped being mission territory administered from Germany. The sagas that tell these stories most vividly were written down two centuries later.
prose_changes.new: Christianity came north in fits and starts over nearly three centuries. A Frankish monk named Anskar preached in Denmark and at Birka in Sweden in the 820s and 830s, with modest and short-lived results. Then came the kings. Harald Bluetooth set up a great carved stone at Jelling claiming that he had 'made the Danes Christian'. In Norway there were the two Olafs. As the sagas tell it, their methods included force, and one of them was killed in battle and venerated as a saint almost at once. Iceland took a different road. In the year 1000 the question was put to the Althing, the island's assembly. The pagan law-speaker Þorgeir thought it over for a night. Then he ruled that all Icelanders should be baptized, though some old practices were allowed in private for a time. A whole community changed its religion by public decision rather than by conquest. The window closes in 1104, when the northern church received its own archbishop at Lund. It stopped being mission ground run from Germany. The sagas that tell these stories most vividly were written down two centuries later.
prose_changes.reason: Ruling 6 guard (violence). The Olafs' forcible methods are stated as the sagas' account, the only witness, which the field already names. Lea (vol. III, lines 18975-18977) reads the sagas the same way for Olaf Tryggvason. Sentences split to meet the reading target.

prose_changes.old: Twice over a century, Byzantine emperors tried to purge Christian worship of images, and both times monks led the resistance, arguing that a God who had become visible in a human being could rightly be painted. Stephen the Younger was killed for the argument in 765, and Theodore of Stoudios was beaten, imprisoned and exiled more than once before icons were restored for good in 843, a day still kept as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.
prose_changes.new: Twice over a century, Byzantine emperors tried to purge Christian worship of images. Both times monks led the resistance. They argued that a God who had become visible in a human being could rightly be painted. Stephen the Younger's Life says he was killed for the argument in 765. Theodore of Stoudios, by his own letters' account, was beaten, imprisoned and exiled more than once. Icons were restored for good in 843, a day still kept as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.
prose_changes.reason: Ruling 6 guard (violence). Neither Stephen's death nor Theodore's sufferings has a source in the Library; each is stated as what its own witness reports (Stephen's Life, Theodore's letters), both on the movement's source list. Sentences split to meet the reading target.

prose_changes.old: Twice over a century and more, the Byzantine court tried to purge Christian worship of images, and both times the strongest organized resistance came from the monasteries. The monks argued that because God had genuinely become a human being who could be seen, he could be depicted — that refusing the image was, in the end, refusing the Incarnation. And they paid for the argument. Stephen the Younger was killed in 765, and Theodore, abbot of the great Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, was beaten, imprisoned and exiled more than once while still producing letters, talks to his monks, and treatises on the holy icons. Images were restored once at the Council of Nicaea in 787 and finally in 843, a day the Orthodox churches still keep as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. One thing is worth knowing about the story as we have it. The winning side wrote the record, and the iconoclasts' own case survives almost entirely in quotations made by the people refuting it.
prose_changes.new: Twice over a century and more, the Byzantine court tried to purge Christian worship of images. Both times the strongest organized resistance came from the monasteries. The monks argued that God had truly become a human being who could be seen, so he could be painted. To refuse the image was, in the end, to refuse the Incarnation. And they paid for the argument. Stephen the Younger, his Life says, was killed in 765. Theodore, abbot of the great Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, tells in his own letters how he was beaten, imprisoned and exiled more than once. Through it all he kept writing letters, talks to his monks, and treatises on the holy icons. Images were restored once at the Council of Nicaea in 787, and for good in 843. The Orthodox churches still keep that day as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. One thing is worth knowing about the story as we have it. The winning side wrote the record. The iconoclasts' own case survives almost entirely in quotations made by the people refuting it.
prose_changes.reason: As the why field. Sentences split to meet the reading target; 'depicted' becomes 'painted'.

prose_changes.old: Byzantine heresy hunters describe the Paulicians as rejecting the Old Testament, the cross and the sacraments, though whether that is what the movement itself believed or what its enemies needed it to believe cannot now be settled, since no Paulician account of their own faith survives. What is certain is what happened to them: after imperial campaigns killed and displaced them, survivors built a fortified state at Tephrike on the Byzantine frontier and raided imperial territory until it fell in 878.
prose_changes.new: Byzantine heresy hunters say the Paulicians rejected the Old Testament, the cross and the sacraments. Whether they truly believed that, or their enemies needed them to, cannot now be settled. No account of their faith in their own words survives. What is certain is what happened to them. Imperial armies killed them and drove them from their homes. The survivors built a fortified state at Tephrike on the frontier. By Byzantine accounts they raided the empire's lands until it fell in 878.
prose_changes.reason: Ruling 6 guard (violence). The imperial killing and uprooting is sourced (Evans 1877, lines 1092-1097, already cited on this movement's links). The Paulician raids are not in that source, so they are given as the Byzantine accounts' claim, in keeping with the field's own point that the record is hostile. Sentences split to meet the reading target.

prose_changes.old: The Paulicians appear in the record between the seventh and ninth centuries in Armenia and eastern Anatolia, and almost everything said about them was written by people trying to destroy them. Byzantine heresy-hunters describe a movement that rejected the Old Testament, the cross, the sacraments and the veneration of Mary, and held a dualist view of the world. Whether that is what the Paulicians believed, or what their enemies needed them to believe, cannot now be settled. What is not in doubt is what was done to them. Imperial campaigns killed and displaced them in large numbers, and the survivors built a fortified state of their own at Tephrike on the frontier, made common cause with the Arabs, and raided Byzantine territory until the fortress fell in 878. Later emperors deported whole Paulician populations to the Balkans.
prose_changes.new: The Paulicians appear in the record from the seventh to the ninth century, in Armenia and eastern Anatolia. Almost everything said about them was written by people trying to destroy them. Byzantine heresy-hunters say the movement rejected the Old Testament, the cross, the sacraments and the honor paid to Mary. They say it held that the world was split between a good power and an evil one. Whether they truly believed that, or their enemies needed them to, cannot now be settled. What is not in doubt is what was done to them. Imperial armies killed and uprooted them in large numbers. The survivors built a fortified state of their own at Tephrike on the frontier, and made common cause with the Arabs. By Byzantine accounts they raided the empire's lands until the fortress fell in 878. Later emperors forced whole Paulician groups to move to the Balkans.
prose_changes.reason: As the why field. Sentences split to meet the reading target; 'deported' kept in substance ('forced ... to move').

prose_changes.old: It never stopped: this is the Roman Catholic Church. The shape the church took here is still, in large part, the shape it has. Its papal primacy is set in law. It has canon law run by trained lawyers, cardinals who elect the pope, and general councils that make law for the whole church. Fourth Lateran's rules on yearly confession and Easter communion shaped lay Catholic life for the next seven centuries. So did darker parts of the same program. The same council made Jews and Muslims in Christian lands wear marked dress. The machinery of inquisition took its lasting form in these decades. The Reformation would later protest against these same claims. John Calvin named Gregory VII as the pope who first won the popes the rank of emperors. The same church carried on into the next era, through Avignon and the Fifth Lateran Council.

prose_changes.old: In 1270 the Solomonic dynasty took the Ethiopian throne, and a wave of monks came with it. Tekle Haymanot and the followers of Ewostatewos led them, and they carried churches deep into newly won lands. The Ewostathians kept Saturday as well as Sunday as a Sabbath. They were persecuted for it for generations, until the emperor Zara Yaqob gave way at a council in 1450. His court chronicle says he ordered the old Sabbath kept as holy as Sunday. The same emperor wrote books of theology. He persecuted the monks of Estifanos when they refused to bow before Mary and the cross. It was all written down in Ge'ez: royal chronicles, saints' lives, hymns to Mary, and the Kebra Nagast. That book gave the dynasty its claim to come down from Solomon and Sheba.

A wave of monks came with it and carried churches deep into newly conquered lands. Two networks led the way: the houses Tekle Haymanot built in Shewa, and the northern houses of the followers of Ewostatewos. The bond between crown and cloister was contested throughout. When the monks of Estifanos refused to bow down before Mary and the cross, he persecuted them. All of it was written down in Ge'ez: royal chronicles, saints' lives, hymns to Mary, and the Kebra Nagast. That book gave the dynasty its Solomonic charter.

prose_changes.old: Across a single century, a scattering of English men and women began writing about the inner life of prayer. They wrote in their own language rather than in Latin. Richard Rolle, the Yorkshire hermit, wrote the Fire of Love. Walter Hilton wrote the Scale of Perfection. An author whose name is lost wrote The Cloud of Unknowing. All of them wrote for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars. Two of the voices are women's. Julian of Norwich was an anchoress, enclosed in a cell beside a Norwich parish church. She spent decades revising an account of sixteen revelations she had received during a near-fatal illness. In the end she reached the line she is still known for: that all shall be well. Margery Kempe was a brewer's wife from Bishop's Lynn, a mother of fourteen who could not write. She dictated to scribes a book about her pilgrimages, her uncontrollable public weeping and the heresy examinations she survived. It is the closest thing the period leaves us to an ordinary believer's own life story. Carthusian monks copied The Cloud and Hilton's Scale and kept them safe.

All of them wrote for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars. Two of the voices are women's. Julian of Norwich was an anchoress, enclosed in a cell beside a Norwich parish church. She spent decades revising an account of sixteen revelations she had received during a near-fatal illness. In the end she reached the line she is still known for: that all shall be well. Margery Kempe was a brewer's wife from Bishop's Lynn who could not write. Her own book says she bore fourteen children. She dictated to scribes a book about her pilgrimages, her uncontrollable public weeping and the heresy examinations she survived. for_mark: Breslau (the case you had in view). Two vendored texts carry it. Nicholas V's letter of June 1447 (Bullarium Franciscanum n.s. I, n. 1072, lines 85929-86186) renews the decrees restricting Jews and Muslims in Italy and makes Capistrano their enforcer. Lea's index (vol. III, lines 37341 and 37378) has 'Jews ... burned by Capistrano in Breslau, ii. 549'. Recommended: the sentences stand as sourced, with 'preaching' dropped (neither text shows it as the cause) and two sourced details added: the 1447 commission and the burning. Option b: keep the old two sentences word for word, sourced as they are. Option c: name Lea in the text. The weak point is that the Breslau witness is one index line; the page it points to is not in the Library (wanted).

John Paul II, 2001 (byzantine-church-after-1054 legacy). Left as written as a plain fact. The era 5 drafter doubts that 'apology' is his word; my own unchecked memory is that he spoke of deep regret and asked forgiveness. No text in the Library settles it, so nothing is changed; the Athens address is wanted.

Margery Kempe, 'a brewer's wife' (the-english-mystics-and-devout). Not part of this ruling's guard, but standard accounts, from her own Book, say she ran a brewery herself. Unchecked here, since the Book is not in the Library. For the entry owner.

Alfred, 'could barely find a priest south of the Thames'. His preface, as usually translated, says he could not remember a single one south of the Thames. The softer wording is not wrong in direction; left for the entry owner.

Date spans ('roughly sixteen centuries', 'nearly eight hundred years later', 'nearly three centuries') are read here as dates, not numbers, since each is worked out from two dates. If you want them guarded as figures, three sentences are affected.
notes: Ruling 6 applied to the logged set only: Open-Gaps 24 (era 2, with its era 3 and era 4 sub-entries), 52 (era 5) and 64 (era 6), with the specific sentences taken from the era audits' Drafting_Record escalations and the era 6 Revision_Round1 restored_facts. 53 facts: 35 plain (stand; wanted text confirmed listed, or added to wants where it was not) and 18 guarded. Of the guarded: 6 sourced (Breslau, Lindisfarne, the Paulicians' persecution, Photius's 279 books, the Kesrwan campaigns, the friars sent to Bosnia), 11 stated as what is reported, each naming its witness (Monte Cassino, the Viking destruction per Alfred, Aelfric's count per his editors, the Olafs per the sagas, Olaf's martyrdom per later writers, Stephen per his Life, Theodore per his letters, the Paulician raids per Byzantine accounts, Lateran IV per its canons, the Ewostathians per their saints' lives, Margery's fourteen per her Book), and 1 (Cluny and the Cistercians) left as already qualified, because it is a relationship and outside this ruling. 'Reported' never weakens a documented act into doubt: no 'alleged', no 'may have'. Movement texts carry no inline citations, so the sources are recorded per fact here. Two sources were added to movement source lists, whose shape (work, type, note) takes them: the Bullarium Franciscanum on the Observant movement and Alcuin's Lindisfarne poem on the Anglo-Saxon movement (prose changes 16-17, field 'sources'; no readability score). The Maronite and Bosnian movements have no source list, so Duwayhi and Fermendzin are recorded here only. Every changed field scores Reading Ease >= 60 and FK <= 10. The era 4 fields (late Anglo-Saxon, Scandinavian, iconophile, Paulician) failed the target before this change, so their long sentences were split to pass; no other fact in them was changed. Quotes are copied from the files at the stated lines, OCR as printed. Near the logged set but outside it, not touched: 'hundreds of Christian rune stones' (scandinavian legacy, a count); Zara Yaqob's persecution of the Estifanos monks (Ethiopian why and longDescription).
